content.title: How Much Do Astronauts Make (Plus Factors That Affect Salary)
content.text: Pay & salaryHow Much Do Astronauts Make (Plus Factors That Affect Salary)What is an astronaut?How much do astronauts make?What increases an astronaut's salary?Requirements for astronautsBecoming an astronaut often takes a lot of determination and time. Typically, there are very few positions available at space agencies, and only highly qualified applicants who meet the physical requirements can make it to the first round of interviews. If you're one of them and would like to know more about some benefits that working as an astronaut can give you, consider learning more about how much you can make in this profession.In this article, we explore the question 'how much do astronauts make?', what factors can increase their salary and explain some requirements and skills of an astronaut.What is an astronaut?An astronaut is a specially trained professional, typically working for the government. Astronauts command, pilot or serve as crew members on spacecraft. Their primary responsibility is to travel into space, participate in spaceflight, space exploration activities and conduct experiments. Astronauts' tasks also include medical and emergency services, maintenance and other operational activities. While on Earth, they go through extensive and tailored astronaut training programmes. It's also common for them to have some public appearances scheduled. Their responsibilities during space exploration missions may also include ensuring the crew's safety, being in charge of the equipment or coordinating in-space physical training sessions. Some astronauts also provide regular maintenance and repairs to satellites. An astronaut's specialisation typically depends on their background and education, but all tasks and duties are equally important. Increasingly, civilian astronauts - non-military individuals - are being included in space missions, as seen with companies like SpaceX and Boeing.Related: The Complete Guide to How To Become an AstronautHow much do astronauts make?You may have wondered 'how much do astronauts make?' when considering a career in science or engineering. Space agencies invest a lot in their employees to make them extensively trained astronauts who can successfully perform experiments in space and fly a spacecraft. The organisations offer them attractive salaries to compensate them for their time and commitment. Here are three of the world's leading space organisations and how much they pay their astronauts:1. UKSA (UK Space Agency)UK Space Agency is one of the few organisations you can consider joining if you aspire to become an astronaut. It leads major programmes to support UK space launches, pioneer satellite innovation and foster aerospace hubs across the Union. The average salary of a UKSA astronaut is £40,000 for starter positions and £86,000 for experienced astronauts.2. ESA (European Space Agency)The organisation that regulates ESA astronaut salaries is the Council of Europe. The council classifies ESA astronaut positions in the A2/A4 grade band of the Coordinated Organisations' salary scale. This means that the average salary for an astronaut at the European Space Agency typically ranges from €6,301 per month to €9,035 per month.3. NASA (The National Aeronautics and Space Administration)The document that indicates the compensation for civilian NASA astronauts is the US Federal Government's General Schedule pay scale. According to the scale, the salaries for NASA astronauts in grades GS-12 through GS-13, which indicate senior mid-level and some top-level positions, start at $65,140 per year and go up to $100,701 per year. The average salary of more experienced top-level astronauts in supervisory positions (grades G-13 through GS-14) starts at $104,898 per year and increases to $161,14 per year. These figures vary depending on paygrade, location and status as federal employees.What increases an astronaut's salary?Astronauts compensation may vary depending on their experience, type of employment or the organisation they work for. Here are some of the most important factors that can impact an astronaut's salary:ExperienceIt's common for experienced astronauts to earn more than their colleagues who're just starting in the field. For example, astronauts like Butch Wilmore and Suni Williams, both of whom have participated in multiple missions, often qualify for higher compensation. Most space agencies offer their employees a starting salary that increases with time, making the job more attractive. There aren't many highly qualified astronauts in the world, so space agencies want to encourage their efforts by continuously trying to make the compensation and work environment more attractive for them. NASA astronauts typically live and train in Houston, a major hub for aerospace and space operations.Related: Work Experience: Definition, Importance and TipsLocationAlthough the world's leading space agencies offer their astronauts similar salaries, relocating can sometimes increase their salaries. For example, a UKSA astronaut who participates in an innovative ESA programme may receive a bonus which significantly influences their income. According to our salary information provided in this article, it's also possible for NASA employees to earn more than astronauts from Europe, even if they have similar responsibilities.BenefitsWorking for a space agency may require frequent work travel or taking part in specialised training sessions abroad. Luckily, most organisations offer their employees various benefits. This may include housing benefits and health insurance. Employee benefits often significantly increase an astronaut's overall compensation and help them feel valued.Participating in international programmesParticipating in international space programmes may help astronauts gain expert knowledge and improve their qualifications. As a result, they may qualify for a higher salary not only during the programme but also when it ends. This is because their local space agencies may decide to promote them or offer them a raise. For example, if you're a UKSA astronaut involved in the EU Space Programme for a duration of time, your salary may be higher than the salary of someone who decides to work exclusively for the UKSA.Requirements for astronautsThe route to becoming an astronaut and working at a space agency is often more complex than in any other profession or industry. This is partly caused by the many requirements that space agencies have for new candidates, which sometimes includes residency, education or physical requirements. For example, if you intend to work at NASA, remember that this is an agency of the United States government. It requires that candidates have United States residency. The organisation also accepts dual residency.To have the chance of working at UKSA or ESA, you usually need a master's degree or higher in medicine, natural sciences, engineering, mathematics or computer science. Typically, all agencies also require candidates to be able to operate and control specialised equipment, have leadership abilities and strong thinking and reasoning skills. On top of this, an astronaut's recruitment process involves a medical check. To pass this, candidates need a high level of fitness and their distant and near visual acuity must be correctable to 20/20 in each eye.Useful skills for astronautsSuccessful astronauts are great leaders who have expert natural and computer science knowledge. Here are some other useful skills that you may need to succeed as an astronaut:Basic astronaut skillsBasic astronaut skills include spacewalking, operating the space station, flying jet planes and controlling a robotic arm. These are all skills astronauts learn during extensive training sessions if they get selected to go into space. If you'd like to improve these skills before joining a space agency, consider theoretical learning first and leave practical training for when you've got access to specialised equipment.Exceptional communication skillsAn astronaut's job may be risky at times, and taking control over unexpected situations requires exceptional communication skills. The ability to communicate quickly and effectively also helps them work better with others. This includes both fellow astronauts and scientists who control specialised equipment during space missions.Related: Types of Communicators at Work (And How To Deal With Them)Quick thinkingThe most successful astronauts can work exceptionally well, both individually and as members of a team. To achieve that, they often use their quick thinking skills, which allows them to analyse complex situations and handle unexpected problems in space. Quick thinking also makes multitasking easier for them. If you'd like to work on your quick thinking, remember that it's a skill closely related to decision-making. This involves assessing and analysing, prioritising or learning how to let go of things that aren't important to you.Computer skillsComputer skills allow astronauts to operate a spacecraft and perform basic duties at an International Space Station, such as monitoring the weather or air pressure. To improve this skill set, astronauts in training work on their analytical thinking and learn about modern technologies used in space. It's also useful for them to know and practice programming because it can strengthen their logical thinking.Related: Computer Skills: Definitions and ExamplesForeign languagesIt's common for space agencies to offer their astronauts international training sessions and participation in international space exploration programmes. To be able to communicate effectively with co-workers from other countries, astronauts need the ability to communicate effectively in foreign languages. For example, if you intend to work on International Space Station, your employer may require you to learn Russian because English and Russian are the two official languages of the ISS.Salary figures reflect data listed on the quoted websites at time of writing. Salaries may vary depending on the hiring organisation and a candidate’s experience, academic background and location.
